# Strategic Research Framework

### Core Objective & Business Context

This study will identify the most important workplace pain points experienced by expecting parents and parents of young children across remote, hybrid, and office-based work arrangements. The goal is to translate those pain points into clear priorities for employer support, workplace policies, manager practices, and benefits.

The timing is important because employers are balancing return-to-office expectations with employee demands for flexibility, while parents are managing childcare, interruptions, work-hour boundaries, performance visibility, and career progression. The research must distinguish between problems caused by the work location itself and problems caused by inflexible norms, poor manager support, or insufficient benefits.

Knowing the answers will help employers decide which interventions to prioritise first, such as flexible hours, predictable meeting norms, childcare support, manager training, phased return-to-work policies, equipment support, or career-protection measures.

### Secondary Research Snapshot

- **Hybrid work is currently preferred by many Indian employees, but actual working patterns lag behind preference.** ACCA’s India Talent Trends 2026 reports that 79% of respondents prefer hybrid work, while 53% are already working in a hybrid model. This supports comparing preferred and current arrangements rather than measuring preference alone. ([dev.accaglobal.com](https://www.dev.accaglobal.com/content/dam/ACCA_Global/professional-insights/GTT-2026/gtt-india-2026-final.pdf))

- **Flexibility is linked to more than location.** ACCA’s India Talent Trends 2025 found that work-life balance, commuting time and cost, and schedule flexibility were key perceived benefits of working from home. The survey should therefore measure control over working hours and predictability, not just remote versus office status. ([accaglobal.com](http://www.accaglobal.com/content/dam/ACCA_Global/professional-insights/Global-talent-trends-2025/PI-GTT-2025-INDIA%20v4.pdf))

- **Office attendance does not resolve the broader employee experience.** JLL’s 2025 India workplace research highlights that employees increasingly expect employers to address well-being, purpose, and personal circumstances alongside physical workplace quality. This supports testing policy and manager behaviours as separate support levers. ([jll.com](https://www.jll.com/en-in/insights/beyond-mandates-the-future-of-work-in-india), [jll.com](https://www.jll.com/en-sa/insights/workforce-preference-barometer))

- **Care work is a significant structural issue in India.** UNDP reports that unpaid care and domestic work in India represent an estimated 15%–17% of GDP, while women continue to carry a disproportionate share of unpaid care work. The questionnaire should allow analysis by parent gender without assuming that all parents experience care responsibilities in the same way. ([undp.org](https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2024-12/undp_brochure_care_project.pdf), [undp.org](https://www.undp.org/india/blog/who-cares-making-care-everyones-work))

- **The key research gap is parent-specific evidence.** Existing workplace studies generally report overall employee preferences. This study should identify which workplace barriers are uniquely severe for expecting parents and parents of young children, and which employer actions are perceived as practical and credible by this audience.

### Research Type & Methodology

- **Study type:** Employee / Internal Research combined with Usage & Attitude and policy-prioritisation research.

- **Stimulus count:** Zero discrete stimuli. The study is not evaluating products, advertisements, concepts, packages, or variants. Cell-based designs such as monadic, A/B, paired comparison, and sequential monadic testing do not apply.

- **Research design:** Linear structured questionnaire using a modular funnel. The survey will move from current work arrangement and recent experiences to pain points, support needs, policy priorities, and recommended actions.

- **Why this approach:** The business decision is about prioritising employer support, not selecting a winning creative or product option. A descriptive design will capture the lived experience of parents across remote, hybrid, and office-based settings while enabling meaningful subgroup comparisons by parent status, work model, and caregiving situation.

- **Alternatives considered:**
  - **Qualitative interviews:** Useful for deeper personal stories, but less suitable as the first step when the organisation needs a prioritised view across several work arrangements.
  - **MaxDiff prioritisation:** Could rank a predefined list of policies, but would be premature before understanding the full range of pain points and whether the policy list reflects respondents’ real needs.
  - **Conjoint or choice-based modelling:** Not chosen because the immediate decision is to diagnose problems and prioritise support areas, not model trade-offs between fully specified policy packages.

- **User control:** If you prefer a different methodology, such as adding qualitative interviews or a follow-up policy prioritisation exercise, it can be changed before the research brief is generated.

- **Survey design logic:** Current behaviour will come before attitudes and policy preferences. The questionnaire will separate current work arrangement from preferred arrangement, ask about concrete recent situations before general satisfaction, and distinguish personal pain points from employer or manager-level causes. Parent groups will be compared without forcing a single definition of the “typical” new parent.

- **Quality controls:** Include platform-compliant attention checks, speeder detection, straight-line response checks, duplicate or inconsistent answer screening, and open-ended gibberish review. Use short screens, fully labelled response scales, and minimal grids for SuperJ mobile and web respondents.

### Target Audience Profile

- **Who we are asking:** Indian adults who are expecting a child, planning parental leave, or parenting a young child while currently working remotely, in a hybrid model, or mainly from an office.

- **Why they matter:** These respondents are directly experiencing the interaction between caregiving demands and workplace expectations. Their answers can reveal whether flexibility is genuinely usable, whether managers respond constructively to interruptions, and whether workplace policies protect productivity, well-being, and career progression.

- **Must-have screening criteria:**
  - Currently employed or actively working in a paid role.
  - Expecting a child, planning parental leave, or caring for at least one young child.
  - Currently working remotely, in a hybrid model, or mainly from an office.
  - Able to describe their recent work and caregiving experience.
  - Capture whether the respondent is the primary caregiver, shares caregiving, or has another regular caregiving arrangement.

- **Important subgroup cuts:** Work arrangement, expecting parent versus parent of a young child, parent gender, primary versus shared caregiving responsibility, access to paid or family childcare, work seniority, and whether the employer currently offers formal support.

- **Fielding context:** Respondents will be reached through verified Indian audiences on the SuperJ mobile application and web. Age, gender, city, and NCCS targeting should be enforced by the audience system before survey entry rather than recollected in the questionnaire.

### Key Information Areas & Data Architecture

- **Current work arrangement and flexibility:** Capture actual work model, expected office attendance, control over start and finish times, and ability to adjust schedules. → Reveals whether the problem is location, schedule control, or both. → Drives recommendations on hybrid policy and flexible-hours design.

- **Caregiving context:** Capture child age or pregnancy stage, caregiving role, childcare availability, and frequency of unexpected care interruptions. → Reveals which parent groups face the greatest operational pressure. → Drives targeted rather than one-size-fits-all support.

- **Work-life boundaries:** Measure after-hours work, meeting spillover, inability to disconnect, schedule unpredictability, and pressure to remain continuously available. → Identifies boundary failures that may exist even in remote work. → Drives meeting, communication, and working-hours norms.

- **Productivity and concentration:** Capture interruptions, suitable workspaces, concentration difficulty, technology limitations, and ability to complete focused work. → Separates environmental barriers from policy or management barriers. → Drives equipment, workspace, focus-time, and workload interventions.

- **Manager and team expectations:** Measure comfort requesting flexibility, perceived response to interruptions, meeting culture, workload allocation, and psychological safety. → Shows whether formal policies are supported by day-to-day behaviour. → Drives manager training and accountability measures.

- **Career growth and visibility:** Capture concerns about promotion, performance evaluation, access to important projects, networking, and visibility while working flexibly or taking leave. → Identifies longer-term career risks beyond immediate workload pain. → Drives return-to-work, performance-review, sponsorship, and progression policies.

- **Employer support priorities:** Present a carefully balanced list of potential support actions after the pain-point diagnosis. → Reveals which interventions are both important and credible to parents. → Drives a prioritised employer action roadmap rather than a broad list of benefits.

### Survey Flow & Question Design Approach

- **Phase 1 — Warm-up and eligibility:** Establish employment status, parent or expecting-parent status, current work model, and recent work recency. Use behavioural screening rather than asking only whether respondents “feel” like working parents.

- **Phase 2 — Current working and caregiving context:** Capture work location, schedule control, childcare arrangements, caregiving role, leave status or plans, and typical points of overlap between work and care. This creates the context needed to interpret later pain-point ratings.

- **Phase 3 — Pain-point diagnosis:** Measure the frequency and severity of childcare interruptions, work-hour boundary issues, concentration problems, manager expectations, technology or workspace barriers, and career visibility concerns. Use fully labelled 5-point scales and concrete time or occurrence anchors where possible.

- **Phase 4 — Support and policy evaluation:** Explore which forms of employer support respondents currently receive, which are actually usable, and where the largest gap exists between support offered and support needed. Keep formal policy availability separate from awareness, access, and perceived usefulness.

- **Phase 5 — Prioritisation and decision close:** Ask respondents to identify the most important employer action, the most urgent problem to solve, and the support that would have the greatest practical impact. Include a concise open-ended question for an example of a policy or manager behaviour that would make work easier.

- **Phase 6 — Optional classification module:** Use existing audience targeting for age, gender, city, and NCCS. Only collect additional classification variables needed for analysis, such as seniority, employment type, caregiving arrangement, and access to childcare.

- **Estimated length:** Approximately 15–25 questions and 8–12 minutes, with routing used to avoid asking expecting parents questions that apply only to parents already caring for a child.

### Expected Insights & Business Decisions Enabled

- **You will be able to:** Identify the most frequent and severe pain points for expecting parents and parents of young children across remote, hybrid, and office-based work.

- **You will be able to:** Separate problems caused by work location from problems caused by unpredictable schedules, team norms, manager behaviour, insufficient childcare support, or career anxiety.

- **You will be able to:** Compare the gap between current work arrangements and preferred arrangements, including whether parents want fully remote work, structured hybrid work, greater schedule control, or better support within office-based work.

- **You will be able to:** Identify which support needs differ between expecting parents, parents of infants, and parents of older young children.

- **You will be able to decide:** Which employer policy changes should receive first priority, such as flexible start and finish times, predictable meeting windows, childcare assistance, phased return-to-work, additional leave, manager training, or equipment support.

- **You will be able to decide:** Whether the primary intervention should be a formal policy change, stronger implementation of existing benefits, manager accountability, or improved communication and access.

- **You will be able to decide:** Which workplace practices may be unintentionally damaging career visibility, promotion confidence, or access to important work for parents using flexible arrangements.

- **Key hypotheses being tested:**
  - Parents experience work-hour unpredictability and boundary erosion as major problems even when they work remotely.
  - Hybrid work is valuable only when office attendance is predictable and compatible with caregiving arrangements.
  - Manager response and team norms may matter more than the formal availability of flexibility.
  - Childcare interruptions create productivity pressure, but career visibility concerns may be the more serious long-term risk.
  - Expecting parents and parents already caring for young children require different forms of employer support.
  - Parents with limited access to paid or family childcare experience greater workplace friction.

- **KPIs to report:**
  - Percentage experiencing each pain point frequently.
  - Average severity score by pain-point area.
  - Current-versus-preferred work arrangement gap.
  - Percentage reporting low control over working hours.
  - Percentage uncomfortable requesting flexibility.
  - Percentage reporting career visibility or progression concerns.
  - Awareness, access, usefulness, and unmet need for existing employer support.
  - Priority share for each proposed policy or support action.
  - Top-ranked urgent problem to solve.
  - Qualitative themes from the open-ended parent experience responses.

turns.research_brief:
# Research Brief: Workplace Flexibility and Pain Points Among New Parents

---

### **Background & Context**

Employers in India are balancing return-to-office expectations with employee demands for flexibility, predictable schedules, and better support for personal circumstances. Current evidence suggests that hybrid work remains preferred by many Indian employees: ACCA reporting indicates that 79% prefer hybrid work, while 53% currently work in a hybrid model. ([economictimes.indiatimes.com](http://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/company/corporate-trends/hybrid-work-to-dominate-but-intentional-office-days-will-define-careers-report/articleshow/131421863.cms), [hr.economictimes.indiatimes.com](https://hr.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/workplace-4-0/workplace-ikigai/hybrid-work-to-dominate-but-intentional-office-days-will-define-careers-report/131438440))

However, workplace location alone may not explain the experience of new parents. JLL’s 2025 workforce research indicates that employees increasingly expect employers to address well-being and personal circumstances alongside the physical workplace, while flexibility remains a major factor in employer choice. ([jll.com](https://www.jll.com/en-in/insights/beyond-mandates-the-future-of-work-in-india), [jll.com](https://www.jll.com/en-in/insights/workforce-preference-barometer))

Care responsibilities create an additional structural challenge. UNDP reports that unpaid care and domestic work in India represent an estimated 15%–17% of GDP, with women carrying a disproportionate share of this work. ([undp.org](https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2024-12/undp_brochure_care_project.pdf), [undp.org](https://www.undp.org/india/blog/who-cares-making-care-everyones-work)) This study will fill the parent-specific evidence gap by identifying which workplace pain points are most frequent and severe, which support measures are actually usable, and which interventions employers should prioritise.

---

### **Research Objectives**

Based on the approved strategic framework, this study will address the following objectives:

#### **Strategic Objectives**

1. **Identify** the most frequent and severe workplace pain points experienced by expecting parents and parents of young children in order to prioritise employer interventions.
2. **Determine** whether workplace difficulties are driven primarily by work location, schedule inflexibility, manager behaviour, team norms, childcare constraints, or inadequate benefits.
3. **Validate** whether flexible work arrangements are genuinely usable for new parents rather than merely available as formal policies.
4. **Assess** the impact of workplace practices on productivity, well-being, work-life boundaries, career visibility, and progression confidence.
5. **Prioritise** the employer policies and manager practices most likely to improve the day-to-day experience of working parents.

#### **Tactical Objectives**

1. **Measure** current and preferred work arrangements across fully remote, hybrid, and mainly office-based employees in order to identify the arrangement gap.
2. **Quantify** control over start times, finish times, meeting schedules, and temporary schedule changes in order to assess practical flexibility.
3. **Map** pregnancy stage, child age, caregiving role, childcare access, and frequency of unexpected care interruptions in order to identify high-friction parent groups.
4. **Measure** the frequency and severity of work-life boundary problems, including after-hours work, meeting spillover, inability to disconnect, and pressure to remain continuously available.
5. **Identify** productivity and concentration barriers, including interruptions, workspace limitations, technology issues, workload pressure, and lack of focused work time.
6. **Assess** manager and team support by measuring comfort requesting flexibility, perceived responses to interruptions, meeting culture, workload allocation, and psychological safety.
7. **Determine** whether parents using flexible arrangements experience concerns about performance evaluation, promotion, important projects, networking, and career visibility.
8. **Measure** awareness, access, usability, and perceived usefulness of existing employer support policies and benefits.
9. **Prioritise** potential interventions such as flexible hours, predictable meeting windows, childcare assistance, phased return-to-work, additional leave, manager training, equipment support, and career-protection measures.
10. **Compare** pain points across expecting parents, parents of infants, parents of older young children, primary caregivers, shared caregivers, and respondents with different childcare access.
11. **Identify** the most urgent workplace problem to solve and the employer action respondents believe would have the greatest practical impact.
12. **Capture** concrete examples of workplace policies or manager behaviours that would make work easier for new parents.

---

### **Type of Study**

We will conduct an **Employee / Internal Research study with Usage & Attitude and policy-prioritisation modules**. This study type is appropriate because the business decision is not to select a product or creative asset, but to diagnose employee experiences and prioritise workplace policies, manager practices, and benefits for expecting parents and parents of young children.

---

### **Survey Design Approach** (Marketing Research Methodology)

The selected approach is a **linear structured questionnaire using a modular funnel**, with zero discrete stimuli and no experimental cells. This fits the objective because respondents will report their current work arrangements, caregiving circumstances, recent workplace experiences, support gaps, and policy priorities. The design will move from behaviour to attitudes and then to prioritisation, reducing recall bias and preventing general satisfaction ratings from replacing concrete experience measures.

The study has **zero discrete stimuli**: there are no concepts, advertisements, products, packages, variants, or price points to compare. Therefore, monadic, sequential monadic, paired-comparison, A/B, and split-cell designs are not appropriate. Policy priorities will be measured through balanced prioritisation questions after the pain-point diagnosis; a full MaxDiff exercise is not required at this stage because the study must first establish whether the proposed policy list reflects respondents’ real needs.

Alternatives considered:

- **Qualitative interviews:** Not selected as the primary design because interviews would provide depth but not a comparable prioritised view across work models and parent groups.
- **MaxDiff / Best-Worst Scaling:** Not selected because the immediate decision is to diagnose the full pain-point landscape before ranking a finalised policy list.
- **Mixed-method follow-up research:** Not selected for the initial phase, but qualitative interviews could be added later to explore the highest-priority pain points in greater depth.

The questionnaire will use fully labelled five-point scales, behavioural anchors, limited grids, forced prioritisation, and targeted open-ended probes. Data quality controls will include attention checks, speedster detection, straight-line response checks, duplicate or inconsistent answer screening, and open-ended gibberish review. Because the audience is Indian, the survey will avoid leading agree/disagree batteries and will use direct, neutral phrasing.

**Survey Routing Logic:**

- **Skip Logic:** Irrelevant pregnancy, childcare, leave, or return-to-work questions will be bypassed.
- **Branching:** Expecting parents and parents already caring for a child will receive relevant paths.
- **Display Logic:** Follow-ups will appear only when respondents report relevant experiences.
- **Termination Logic:** Respondents who are not currently working or do not meet the parent or expecting-parent criteria will exit gracefully.
- **Completion Logic:** The survey will close once all relevant modules are completed.
- **Quality Controls:** Attention checks will appear at approximately a 1:9 ratio, with speedster detection below 40%–50% of median completion time and straight-line detection across rating batteries.

You can request a different methodology before generating the survey.

---

### **Question Flow & Survey Phases**

The survey will use a short, mobile-friendly funnel of approximately 15–25 questions and 8–12 minutes.

- **Phase 1 — Warm-Up and Eligibility:** Confirm current employment, paid-work status, expecting-parent or parent status, child-care responsibility, work recency, and current work model. This establishes eligibility without collecting demographic information already enforced by audience targeting.
- **Phase 2 — Work and Caregiving Context:** Capture actual work location, expected office attendance, schedule control, pregnancy stage or child age, caregiving role, childcare access, leave status, and typical work-care overlap.
- **Phase 3 — Recent Workplace Experiences:** Measure concrete recent experiences involving interruptions, meetings, after-hours work, schedule changes, concentration, workspace, technology, workload, and ability to disconnect.
- **Phase 4 — Manager, Team, and Career Experience:** Assess comfort requesting flexibility, manager responses, psychological safety, workload allocation, performance visibility, promotion confidence, access to important work, and career progression concerns.
- **Phase 5 — Employer Support and Policy Prioritisation:** Measure awareness, access, usability, and usefulness of existing support, followed by prioritisation of potential employer interventions.
- **Phase 6 — Decision Close:** Identify the most urgent problem to solve, the single most valuable employer action, and one concise example of a policy or manager behaviour that would improve the respondent’s experience.

---

### **Key Data Points to Measure**

#### **Primary Metrics**

- **Current work arrangement** - enables comparison across remote, hybrid, and office-based employees.
- **Preferred work arrangement** - quantifies the gap between current and desired working models.
- **Expected office attendance** - assesses predictability and compatibility with caregiving routines.
- **Control over working hours** - identifies whether flexibility is operationally usable.
- **Frequency of unexpected care interruptions** - measures the practical collision between work and caregiving.
- **Severity of workplace pain points** - identifies the problems requiring the fastest employer response.
- **Work-life boundary erosion** - measures after-hours work, meeting spillover, inability to disconnect, and continuous-availability pressure.
- **Productivity and concentration difficulty** - assesses interruptions, workspace constraints, technology barriers, and focused-work limitations.
- **Comfort requesting flexibility** - measures psychological safety and perceived risk when using flexibility.
- **Manager response to caregiving needs** - distinguishes formal policy availability from day-to-day implementation.
- **Team and meeting norms** - identifies whether workplace practices create avoidable friction.
- **Career visibility concern** - measures perceived impact on performance evaluation, promotion, networking, and access to important work.
- **Existing support awareness** - identifies communication and discoverability gaps.
- **Support access and usefulness** - separates policy availability from actual usability and value.
- **Policy priority share** - identifies the employer interventions with the greatest perceived practical impact.
- **Most urgent problem to solve** - creates a clear leadership-level prioritisation metric.

#### **Supporting Metrics**

- Parent status: expecting parent, parent of an infant, or parent of an older young child.
- Pregnancy stage, where relevant.
- Child age bands, where relevant.
- Primary caregiver, shared caregiver, or another regular caregiving arrangement.
- Access to paid childcare, family childcare, informal care, or no regular childcare.
- Frequency of childcare coverage changes or unexpected care gaps.
- Employment type and work seniority.
- Formal parental or caregiver support currently offered by the employer.
- Whether the respondent has taken, is taking, or is planning parental leave.
- Perceived impact of flexibility on well-being, productivity, and career progression.
- Open-ended themes describing helpful or harmful policies and manager behaviours.

#### **Advanced Analytics We'll Apply**

- **Cross-tabulation** to compare pain points by work arrangement, parent status, gender, caregiving role, childcare access, seniority, and employer support availability.
- **Gap analysis** to compare current versus preferred work arrangements and support offered versus support needed.
- **Severity-frequency mapping** to identify pain points that are both widespread and damaging.
- **Driver analysis** to assess whether manager support, schedule control, or childcare access is most associated with overall workplace experience.
- **Segment profiling** to identify practical groups such as flexibility-constrained parents, childcare-constrained parents, career-anxious flexible workers, and adequately supported parents.
- **Open-ended thematic and sentiment analysis** to identify recurring examples of effective or ineffective policies and manager behaviours.
- **Priority ranking analysis** to create an employer action roadmap.

---

### **Expected Insights & Outcomes**

By the end of this study, you will possess the data to:

- **Validate:** Whether parents experience work-hour unpredictability and boundary erosion as major problems even when working remotely.
- **Validate:** Whether hybrid work is valuable only when office attendance is predictable and compatible with caregiving arrangements.
- **Validate:** Whether manager response and team norms matter more than the formal availability of flexibility.
- **Validate:** Whether childcare interruptions create immediate productivity pressure while career visibility concerns represent the more serious long-term risk.
- **Validate:** Whether expecting parents and parents already caring for young children require different forms of employer support.
- **Validate:** Whether parents with limited access to paid or family childcare experience greater workplace friction.
- **Determine:** Which pain points are most frequent and severe across remote, hybrid, and office-based work.
- **Determine:** Whether the primary intervention should be a formal policy change, stronger implementation of existing benefits, manager accountability, or improved communication and access.
- **Decide:** Which employer policy changes should receive first priority, including flexible start and finish times, predictable meeting windows, childcare assistance, phased return-to-work, additional leave, manager training, equipment support, and career-protection measures.
- **Decide:** Which support needs differ between expecting parents, parents of infants, and parents of older young children.
- **Decide:** Whether workplace practices are unintentionally damaging career visibility, promotion confidence, or access to important work for parents using flexible arrangements.
- **Strategize:** How to design support around specific caregiving situations rather than applying a one-size-fits-all policy.
- **Strategize:** How to align formal workplace policies with manager behaviour, team norms, and communication practices.

**Key hypotheses being tested:**

1. Parents experience work-hour unpredictability and boundary erosion as major problems even when they work remotely.
2. Hybrid work is valuable only when office attendance is predictable and compatible with caregiving arrangements.
3. Manager response and team norms may matter more than the formal availability of flexibility.
4. Childcare interruptions create productivity pressure, but career visibility concerns may be the more serious long-term risk.
5. Expecting parents and parents already caring for young children require different forms of employer support.
6. Parents with limited access to paid or family childcare experience greater workplace friction.

**KPIs to report:**

- Percentage experiencing each pain point frequently.
- Average severity score by pain-point area.
- Current-versus-preferred work arrangement gap.
- Percentage reporting low control over working hours.
- Percentage uncomfortable requesting flexibility.
- Percentage reporting career visibility or progression concerns.
- Awareness, access, usefulness, and unmet need for existing employer support.
- Priority share for each proposed policy or support action.
- Top-ranked urgent problem to solve.
- Qualitative themes from open-ended parent experience responses.

---

### **Methodology** [See why](hercules://explain?topic=Methodology)

We will deploy an **approximately 20-question, 8–12-minute** linear structured survey on the **SuperJ mobile application and the web** to **500 verified Indian respondents**.

The sample will be a single non-cell design because there are no discrete stimuli to compare. The questionnaire will begin with eligibility and current behaviour, continue into caregiving and workplace experiences, and finish with support evaluation and policy prioritisation. Routing will prevent expecting parents from receiving irrelevant questions about current childcare, while parents of young children will receive the relevant caregiving path.

A sample of 500 respondents provides a strong directional read for the defined audience and supports subgroup comparisons across work model, parent status, caregiving responsibility, childcare access, and employer support availability. Results will be interpreted as survey estimates for the targeted audience rather than as a national probability estimate.

The question mix will combine behavioural frequency measures, fully labelled five-point severity and usefulness scales, forced prioritisation, and open-ended probes only at high-value decision points. Data collection will use verified Indian respondents with age, gender, city, and NCCS targeting enforced before survey entry.

**Data Collection Approach:** SuperJ mobile application and web panel, with audience targeting enforced before survey start.

**Quality Controls:** Attention checks, speeder removal, straight-line detection, duplicate and inconsistency screening, and open-ended gibberish filtering.

---

### **Target Audience** [See why](hercules://explain?topic=Target+Audience)

The study will target **Indian adults who are expecting a child, planning parental leave, or parenting a young child while currently working in a paid role**. Respondents may currently work remotely, in a hybrid model, or mainly from an office. They must be able to describe recent experiences involving work, caregiving, flexibility, manager support, and workplace policies.

**Total Sample Size:** 500 respondents

**Geographic Focus:** Delhi, Mumbai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, and Pune. These five cities provide a focused spread of major Indian employment markets without scattering the sample across too many locations.

**Demographics:**

- **Gender:** 50% Male / 50% Female.
- **Age Range:** 24-35 and 35-45. The 24-35 bracket will represent 300 respondents and the 35-45 bracket will represent 200 respondents.
- **Socioeconomic Class:** NCCS A1, A2, A3, B1, and B2, with a balanced mix to capture employed parents across higher and middle socioeconomic groups.

**Behavioral and Caregiving Filters:**

- Currently employed or actively working in a paid role.

survey_objectives.importance: Leadership needs a common outcome benchmark against which workplace pain points, flexibility experiences, and support interventions can be evaluated.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure current work model and parent-life-stage eligibility across remote, hybrid, and mainly office-based respondents to compare workplace experiences by work arrangement and caregiving situation.
survey_objectives.importance: The business must distinguish location-related problems from broader flexibility and caregiving barriers.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure role clarity, growth opportunity, career visibility, and progression concerns among expecting parents and parents of young children.
survey_objectives.importance: Career penalties may create longer-term retention and equity risks even when day-to-day flexibility is available.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure manager effectiveness, psychological safety, comfort raising caregiving needs, and manager behaviours that should be amplified.
survey_objectives.importance: Formal flexibility may remain unusable if managers respond negatively or inconsistently to caregiving needs.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure belonging and teamwork quality to assess whether team norms and collaboration practices create avoidable friction for working parents.
survey_objectives.importance: Team behaviour can determine whether flexible arrangements work in practice.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure alignment with organizational values, perceptions of culture, and the single cultural or policy change respondents most want.
survey_objectives.importance: The business needs bottom-up evidence to design credible, parent-supportive culture and policy changes.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure workload manageability and work-life balance, including schedule unpredictability, boundary erosion, care interruptions, productivity barriers, wellbeing impact, and work-care overlap through compact sub-items.
survey_objectives.importance: These measures identify whether workplace practices are damaging wellbeing, concentration, productivity, and the ability to disconnect.

survey_objectives.objective: Measure whether contributions are recognized and whether workplace fairness is perceived, including compensation and treatment of employees using flexibility.
survey_objectives.importance: Perceived unfairness can weaken engagement and increase the risk that parents leave the organization.

business_flow.questionnaire_intent: Use an empathetic, anonymous, mobile-friendly organizational-health questionnaire with exactly 20 respondent-facing question keys. The flow begins with parent eligibility and current work model, then measures engagement, role and growth, manager and team experience, culture, wellbeing, and recognition; compact grids and targeted open-ended components capture the broader parent-workplace diagnostic within the fixed budget.

questionnaire_sections.purpose: Establish parent eligibility, current work model, overall engagement, pride, and retention baseline. Supports objectives 1 and 2.

Measure role clarity, growth, career visibility, practical flexibility, pain-point frequency and severity, caregiving context, childcare access, and policy barriers using compact sub-items within the three mandated questions. Supports objectives 2, 3, 7, and 9.

Measure manager effectiveness, psychological safety, comfort requesting flexibility, responses to caregiving needs, and positive manager behaviours through the mandated manager measures. Supports objective 4.
Measure belonging, teamwork quality, meeting norms, collaboration friction, and team support for caregiving through the two mandated team measures. Supports objective 5.
Measure value alignment, culture perception, the most urgent cultural change, and bottom-up policy or manager ideas through the mandated culture measures. Supports objectives 6 and 9.

Measure workload manageability, boundary erosion, care interruptions, productivity barriers, work-life balance, wellbeing, and work-care overlap through compact sub-items within the two mandated measures. Supports objectives 7 and 8.

Measure recognition, fairness, support awareness and usefulness, unmet needs, policy priorities, urgent problem, greatest-impact action, and a concise concrete example through compact sub-items within the two mandated measures. Supports objectives 8 and 9 and closes the survey.

question_generation_instructions: METHODOLOGY: Employee Engagement — Organizational Health Methodology. Preserve the seven sections and exact order: Overall Engagement, Role & Growth, Manager Relationship, Team & Collaboration, Culture & Values, Wellbeing & Workload, and Recognition & Fairness. Use exactly 20 respondent-facing question keys, with no stimuli or experimental cells.
Use the mandated flow keys exactly as provided. Do not add demographic targeting keys or additional respondent-facing keys.

Use PARENT_STATUS as a combined eligibility and life-stage screener so the exact 20-question budget is maintained. Include expecting-parent, current-parent, not-working, and none-of-these response paths.
Keep the tone empathetic, anonymous, neutral, and no-blame. Avoid leading agree/disagree batteries.

Use compact grids and structured sub-items to capture current/preferred work arrangement, schedule control, childcare access, care interruptions, pain-point frequency and severity, boundary erosion, productivity barriers, career visibility, policy awareness/access/usefulness, and unmet need without adding question keys.

Implement the advanced techniques: include a stay/leave or retention-risk signal through RETENTION_INTENT, a workplace/career risk signal within ROLE_CLARITY or GROWTH_OPPORTUNITY, and a bottom-up policy or manager-behaviour example within CULTURE_CHANGE or the closing recognition/fairness module.
Measure behavior before attitudes, attitudes before prioritisation, and place the most valuable open-ended example late in the questionnaire.
Use fully labelled five-point scales, behavioral anchors, limited grids, forced prioritisation, and concise open-ended probes suitable for an 8–12 minute mobile survey.
Cross-tab results by current work model, parent life stage, caregiving situation, childcare access, and audience-payload age/gender fields without recollecting those database variables.
Complete the survey after the Recognition & Fairness section. Quality failures must be classified separately from ordinary eligibility screen-outs.

termination_and_completion_policy.condition: PARENT_STATUS indicates that the respondent is not currently working in a paid role.
PARENT_STATUS indicates None of these: the respondent is neither expecting a child, planning parental leave, nor parenting a young child.
CURRENT_WORK_MODEL indicates Other arrangement.
A pregnancy, child-age, childcare, leave, return-to-work, care-interruption, or career-risk sub-item does not apply to the respondent's parent-life-stage or reported experience.
Respondent fails an attention check or quality screen based on speed, straight-lining, duplication, inconsistency, or unusable open-ended content.
Respondent completes all applicable content through the recognition, support, prioritisation, and decision-close components within RECOGNITION_FAIRNESS.
